items.readable_text:
Content:
A set is a collection of objects known as elements or members.

Content:
Usually, the elements of a set have some property in common. For example, a set could be a class at school where the students are the members of the set. The common property is that all the students are members of the class.

Content:
To write a set, we list the elements between two braces (curly brackets). Commas are used to separate the elements.

Content:
So, for example, the set of the primary colors would be written as

Content:
[MATH: S =\{ \text{yellow}, \: \text{red}, \: \text{blue} \}.]

Content:
The elements of this set are [MATH: \text{yellow},] [MATH: \text{red},] and [MATH: \text{blue}.]

Content:
A set that does not contain any elements is known as the null set or empty set and is written as either
[MATH: \emptyset \quad \text{or} \quad \{\}.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- A set may contain other sets as elements. For instance, the set
[MATH: T = \{1, \: 2, \: 3, \: 4, \: \{5, 6\}\}]
contains the set [MATH: \{5, 6\}] as an element. However, it does not contain the elements [MATH: 5] and [MATH: 6].
- Order doesn't matter. The order in which the elements are listed is irrelevant. For instance, the following sets represent the same thing:
[MATH: A = \{1, \: 2, \: 3 \} = \{2, \: 3, \: 1\}]
It's usually easier to understand a set if the elements are listed in some order.
- Duplicates don't matter. Having multiple copies of an element does not affect the structure of a set. For example, the following sets represent the same thing:
[MATH: B = \{m, \: n, \: p, \: q\} = \{m, \: m, \: m, \: n, \: n, \: p, \: p, \: p, \: q\}]
When writing a set, we should try to organize it so that each element is listed once only.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A set is a collection of elements listed between two braces (curly brackets). However, note that the null set (the set that does not contain any elements) can be written as either [MATH: \{\}] or [MATH: \emptyset.]

  • [MATH: \{ \{ 2 \}, \{ 4, 6 \} \}] is a set. The elements are [MATH: \{ 2 \}] and [MATH: \{ 4, 6 \},] and are listed between the two outermost braces.

  • [MATH: 2, 4, 6] is not a set. The numbers [MATH: 2,] [MATH: 4,] and [MATH: 6] are not listed between two braces.

  • [MATH: \emptyset] is the empty set. Therefore, it is a set.

In conclusion, only III is not a set.

Content:

Content:

Content:
Finally, note that [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] contain a finite number of elements ([MATH: A] and [MATH: B] contain [MATH: 9] and [MATH: 99] elements, respectively), while [MATH: C] contains infinitely many elements:

Content:
- A set containing a finite number of elements is called a finite set.
- A set containing an infinite number of elements is called an infinite set.

Content:
So, [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are finite sets, while [MATH: C] is an infinite set.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A set is a collection of objects known as elements or members.

Content:
Usually, the elements of a set have some property in common. For example, a set could be a class at school where the students are the members of the set. The common property is that all the students are members of the class.

Content:
To write a set, we list the elements between two braces (curly brackets). Commas are used to separate the elements.

Content:
So, for example, the set of the primary colors would be written as

Content:
[MATH: S =\{ \text{yellow}, \: \text{red}, \: \text{blue} \}.]

Content:
The elements of this set are [MATH: \text{yellow},] [MATH: \text{red},] and [MATH: \text{blue}.]

Content:
A set that does not contain any elements is known as the null set or empty set and is written as either
[MATH: \emptyset \quad \text{or} \quad \{\}.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- A set may contain other sets as elements. For instance, the set
[MATH: T = \{1, \: 2, \: 3, \: 4, \: \{5, 6\}\}]
contains the set [MATH: \{5, 6\}] as an element. However, it does not contain the elements [MATH: 5] and [MATH: 6].
- Order doesn't matter. The order in which the elements are listed is irrelevant. For instance, the following sets represent the same thing:
[MATH: A = \{1, \: 2, \: 3 \} = \{2, \: 3, \: 1\}]
It's usually easier to understand a set if the elements are listed in some order.
- Duplicates don't matter. Having multiple copies of an element does not affect the structure of a set. For example, the following sets represent the same thing:
[MATH: B = \{m, \: n, \: p, \: q\} = \{m, \: m, \: m, \: n, \: n, \: p, \: p, \: p, \: q\}]
When writing a set, we should try to organize it so that each element is listed once only.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying the Elements of a Set

Example Prompt:
List the elements of the following set:
[MATH: A = \big\{a, c,3, \{c,3 \}, \emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\big\}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The elements of the set [MATH: A] are as follows:

[MATH: a, \quad c, \quad 3, \quad \{c,3\}, \quad \emptyset, \quad \{\emptyset\}]

Watch Out!

- The elements [MATH: c,3,] and [MATH: \{c,3\}] are three separate entities. The first two are the elements [MATH: c] and [MATH: 3,] and the third is a set containing these two elements.
- The elements [MATH: \emptyset] and [MATH: \{ \emptyset \}] are also separate entities. The first one is the empty set (i.e., the set containing no elements), while the second is a set that contains the empty set.

---

Item 3 — Question 1

Prompt:
Which of the following is an element of the set [MATH: A = {a, b, c, e}?]

Choices:
a. [MATH: 1]
b. [MATH: 2]
c. [MATH: d]
d. [MATH: c]
e. [MATH: ♣]

---

Item 4 — Question 2

Prompt:
Which of the following is an element of the set [MATH: C = {{a}, b, {c}, d, {e}}?]

Choices:
a. [MATH: e]
b. [MATH: a]
c. [MATH: c]
d. [MATH: {e}]
e. [MATH: {d}]

---

Item 5 — Question 3

Prompt:
Which of the following is not an element of the set [MATH: B = {∅, 1, {∅}, {1}}?]

Choices:
a. [MATH: {∅, 1}]
b. [MATH: 1]
c. [MATH: ∅]
d. [MATH: {∅}]
e. [MATH: {1}]

---

Item 6 — Example: Identifying Non-Sets

Example Prompt:
Which of the following is not a set?

1. [MATH: \{ 2, 4, 6 \}]
2. [MATH: \{ \{ 2 \}, \{ 4, 6 \} \}]
3. [MATH: 2, 4, 6]
4. [MATH: \emptyset]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A set is a collection of elements listed between two braces (curly brackets). However, note that the null set (the set that does not contain any elements) can be written as either [MATH: \{\}] or [MATH: \emptyset.]

- [MATH: \{ 2, 4, 6 \}] is a set. The elements are [MATH: 2,] [MATH: 4,] and [MATH: 6,] and they are listed between two braces.
- [MATH: \{ \{ 2 \}, \{ 4, 6 \} \}] is a set. The elements are [MATH: \{ 2 \}] and [MATH: \{ 4, 6 \},] and are listed between the two outermost braces.
- [MATH: 2, 4, 6] is not a set. The numbers [MATH: 2,] [MATH: 4,] and [MATH: 6] are not listed between two braces.
- [MATH: \emptyset] is the empty set. Therefore, it is a set.

In conclusion, only III is not a set.

---

Item 7 — Question 4

Prompt:
Which of the following is not a set?

Choices:
a. [MATH: {{− 2}, (1)/(2)}]
b. [MATH: {(5)/(2), 6, 7}]
c. [MATH: {∅, {(1)/(5)}}]
d. [MATH: 8, − (1)/(2)]
e. [MATH: {{− 2}}]

---

Prompt:
Which of the following is not a set?

Choices:
a. [MATH: {}]
b. [MATH: {1, 1, 2}]
c. [MATH: 1, 2, 3]
d. [MATH: {1, 2, 3}]
e. [MATH: {1}]

---

Item 9 — Question 6

Prompt:
Which of the following is not a set?

Choices:
a. [MATH: ∅]
b. [MATH: {{}}]
c. [MATH: {}]
d. [MATH: (1)/(2), (1)/(3), (1)/(4), (1)/(5)]
e. [MATH: {(1)/(2), (1)/(3), (1)/(4), (1)/(5)}]

---

Item 10 — Tutorial: Element Notation

Content:
By convention, sets are denoted by uppercase letters, while lowercase letters refer to elements of the set.

Content:
There is a special notation, [MATH: \in,] for expressing elements of sets. For example, if [MATH: a] is an element of a set [MATH: A,] we write

Content:
[MATH: a \in A.]

Content:
For example, for the set [MATH: S,] given by

Content:
[MATH: S = \{ \text{yellow}, \text{red}, \text{blue} \},]
we can write

Content:
[MATH: \text{yellow}\in S.]

Content:
Similarly, if [MATH: a] is not an element of [MATH: A,] then we write

Content:
[MATH: a \notin A.]

Content:
For example,

Content:
[MATH: \text{green} \notin S.]

---

Item 11 — Example: Using Element Notation

Example Prompt:
Write the following statement using element notation:

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: 1] and [MATH: 2] are elements of a set [MATH: S,] but [MATH: 3,] [MATH: 4,] and [MATH: 5] are not.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If [MATH: a] is an element of [MATH: S,] we write [MATH: a \in S.] Otherwise, if [MATH: a] is not an element of [MATH: S,] we write [MATH: a \notin S.]

- Since [MATH: 1] and [MATH: 2] are elements of [MATH: S,] we write [MATH: 1,2 \in S.]
- Since [MATH: 3,] [MATH: 4,] and [MATH: 5] are not elements of [MATH: S,] we write [MATH: 3,4,5 \notin S.]

All together, we have the following statement:

[MATH: 1,2 \in S\quad \textrm{and}\quad 3,4,5 \notin S]

---

Item 12 — Question 7

Prompt:
If [MATH: (1)/(2), (1)/(3),] and [MATH: (1)/(4)] are elements of [MATH: A,] but [MATH: (1)/(3)] is not an element of [MATH: B,] then which of the following is true?

Choices:
a. [MATH: (1)/(2), (1)/(3), (1)/(4) ∈ A] and [MATH: (1)/(3) ∉ B]
b. [MATH: (1)/(2), (1)/(4) ∈ A] and [MATH: (1)/(3), (1)/(4) ∉ B]
c. [MATH: (1)/(2), (1)/(3), (1)/(4) ∉ B]
d. [MATH: (1)/(2), (1)/(3), (1)/(4) ∈ A] and [MATH: (1)/(3) ∈ B]
e. [MATH: (1)/(3) ∉ A] and [MATH: (1)/(2), (1)/(3), (1)/(4) ∈ B]

Item 13 — Question 8

Prompt:
If [MATH: a, b,] and [MATH: c] are elements of [MATH: S], but [MATH: d] and [MATH: e] are not, then which of the following is true?

Choices:
a. [MATH: a, b ∈ S] and [MATH: c, d, e ∉ S]
b. [MATH: a, b, c ∉ S] and [MATH: d, e ∈ S]
c. [MATH: d, e ∈ S]
d. [MATH: a, b, c ∈ S] and [MATH: d, e ∉ S]
e. [MATH: a, b, c ∉ S]

---

Item 14 — Tutorial: Ellipsis Notation

Content:
When a set contains only a few elements, we can write them all explicitly.

Content:
For example, the set [MATH: A] containing all positive even integers less than [MATH: 20] could be written as follows:

Content:
[MATH: A = \{2, \: 4, \: 6, \: 8, \: 10, \: 12, \: 14, \: 16, \: 18\}]

Content:
However, when a set contains many elements, we can save ourselves the pain of writing out all its elements using an ellipsis, "[MATH: \ldots]".

Content:
For example:

Content:
- The set [MATH: B] containing all positive even integers less than [MATH: 200] can be written as
[MATH: B = \{2, \: 4, \: 6, \: \ldots, \: 198\}.]
- The set [MATH: C] containing all positive even integers can be written as
[MATH: C = \{ 2, \: 4, \: 6, \: \ldots \}.]

Content:
Generally, an ellipsis means "and so on up to" if it's followed by a specific element or "and so on" if not.

Content:
Finally, note that [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] contain a finite number of elements ([MATH: A] and [MATH: B] contain [MATH: 9] and [MATH: 99] elements, respectively), while [MATH: C] contains infinitely many elements:

Content:
- A set containing a finite number of elements is called a finite set.
- A set containing an infinite number of elements is called an infinite set.

Content:
So, [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] are finite sets, while [MATH: C] is an infinite set.

---

- The set [MATH: X] of all positive integers greater than or equal to [MATH: 10]
- The set [MATH: Y] of integers less than zero
- The set [MATH: A] of all natural numbers greater than [MATH: 5] and less than [MATH: 5\, 005]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Remember that an ellipsis means "and so on up to" if it's followed by a specific element, or "and so on" if not.

- To express the set [MATH: X,] we start with the first positive integer greater than or equal to [MATH: 10,] which is [MATH: 10.] The next integer is [MATH: 11,] the one after that is [MATH: 12,] and so on, which we denote with an ellipsis:
[MATH: X = \{10, 11, 12, \ldots \}]
- To express the set [MATH: Y,] we start with the first integer less than zero, which is [MATH: -1.] The next integer less than zero is [MATH: -2,] the one after that is [MATH: -3,] and so on, which we denote with an ellipsis:
[MATH: Y = \{ -1, -2, -3, \ldots \}]
However, note that it is conventional to write a set of numbers from least to greatest, just like is shown on the number line. Writing the elements of [MATH: Y] from least to greatest, we have
[MATH: Y = \{ \ldots , -3, -2, -1\}.]
- To express the set [MATH: A,] we start with the first positive integer greater than [MATH: 5,] which is [MATH: 6.] The next integer is [MATH: 7,] the one after that is [MATH: 8,] and so on up to [MATH: 5\, 004] (the largest integer less than [MATH: 5\, 005]). So, we have
[MATH: A = \{6, 7, 8, \ldots , 5004\}.]
